name: delibsim-bench
description: delib-sim-bench is a benchmark of multi-agent LLM deliberation simulations. It contains pre/post Deliberative Reason Index (DRI) survey responses, deliberation transcripts, AQuA discourse-quality scores, and full simulation configurations across 11 model setups (single-model and mixed-model, with and without reasoning), 12 policy topics, and 3 prompt conditions (control_1, control_2, treatment), plus five secondary studies varying agent count, persona use, prompt design, deliberation rounds, and temperature. See DATASHEET.md (Gebru et al. style) for the full datasheet.

creator.name: Anonymous
creator.description: Authors anonymized for double-blind NeurIPS 2026 submission.

dataLimitations: Reasoning-trace transcripts (*_with_reasoning.txt) are intentionally excluded from the released bundle to keep the download small. Only the public-facing turn text is shipped.

control_1 is a no-deliberation baseline condition used to estimate intrinsic DRI survey re-test noise. By design, no agent discussion is run in control_1; therefore transcript fields and transcript files are empty for these runs. Consequently, discourse-quality analysis (AQuA) is only defined for conditions where deliberation exists (control_2 and treatment).
AQuA discourse-quality scoring is itself produced by an LLM (separate from the deliberation agents) and inherits its noise and biases. Per-turn quality-index 0/1 indicators are not human-validated.

LLM output drifts over time. The snapshot reflects model versions available via OpenRouter between November 2025 and March 2026; exact reproduction of agent responses requires the same model snapshots, which providers may deprecate.

All deliberations are conducted in English. The 12 deliberation topics are predominantly Western policy debates (Australia, Switzerland, Sweden, Germany); generalisation to non-Western contexts and other languages is unverified.

The benchmark is not recommended for: (a) drawing conclusions about human deliberative behaviour (agents are LLMs, not humans); (b) real-world policy decisions on the 12 topics (agent positions are model artefacts, not citizen views); (c) training models to imitate specific human individuals (no such data exists in the bundle); (d) claims about 'deliberative AI' replacing human deliberation.
dataBiases: Model bias: agents inherit the political, cultural, and linguistic training biases of their underlying LLMs. All models in the main grid are commercially trained on predominantly Western internet text.

Topic bias: the 12 topics are skewed toward Anglophone-Western deliberative-democracy traditions, with Australia over-represented (acp, auscj, bep, biobanking_wa, ccps, energy_futures, fnqcj, forestera, fremantle = 9 of 12). Switzerland (swiss_health), Sweden (uppsala_speaks), and Germany (zukunft) make up the remaining 3.

Selection bias on models: only commercially-served LLMs accessible via OpenRouter at the time of data collection are included. Smaller open-weight models, fine-tuned variants, and self-hosted models are not represented.

Sycophantic-agreement bias: contemporary instruction-tuned LLMs are known to over-agree under multi-turn discussion conditions. Apparent post-deliberation consensus measured by ΔDRI may therefore inflate genuine deliberative impact relative to human-only deliberation.

AQuA-scorer normative bias: the AQuA quality indicators operationalise Habermasian deliberation theory (justification, respect, reference to common good, etc.). Communities that value other deliberative norms (consensus-building over argumentation, oral / narrative traditions, ritualised disagreement) will score artificially low on these indicators.

Prompt bias: deliberation prompts are written in English and frame the deliberation as a Western citizen-assembly-style process; agents are therefore biased toward Anglophone discourse norms regardless of the underlying model.
personalSensitiveInformation: No personal or sensitive information is contained in the dataset. All deliberators are LLM agents; no human subjects participated at any stage of data collection. The agents' role-played expressions of opinion on policy topics are model artefacts and do not reflect the views of any real person, organisation, or community.

No personally identifying information about the dataset's authors, API account holders, or any third party is present in the shipped files. Absolute filesystem paths from the original collection machine were stripped during anonymisation (see claude/dataset/anonymize.py).
dataUseCases: Construct: 'deliberative reason' (DRI) operationalises intersubjective consistency on a policy question across agents and time. Construct validity established for: ranking LLMs on deliberative impact (ΔDRI), comparing prompt conditions (control vs. treatment), and comparing reasoning vs. non-reasoning model variants under identical conditions.

Construct: 'discourse quality' (AQuA) operationalises Habermasian deliberation criteria via per-turn 0/1 indicators across 20 quality categories. Construct validity established for: ranking transcripts on aggregate quality, identifying low-quality transcripts for filtering, and training discourse-quality classifiers.
- benchmarking LLMs on deliberative quality and impact
- studying treatment effects of normative deliberation prompts
- comparing reasoning vs non-reasoning model variants
- methodological work on multi-agent LLM deliberation simulation (group size, persona, prompt design, rounds, temperature)
- training transcript-quality classifiers using the per-turn AQuA indicators as supervised signals
Use cases for which validity has NOT been established:
- drawing conclusions about human deliberative behaviour from these LLM-generated deliberations
- using ΔDRI as a proxy for the social impact of any deployed deliberation system
- cross-cultural deliberation research (the dataset is monolingual English and Western-centric)
- safety / alignment evaluation (DRI and AQuA are not safety metrics)
dataSocialImpact: Positive impact: provides a standardised benchmark for measuring deliberative quality and impact across LLMs, enabling more principled comparisons between model families and prompt designs. Supports methodological research on whether automated deliberation can augment human deliberative processes such as citizen assemblies, policy consultations, and structured public engagement. Releases all transcripts, configurations, and per-turn scores under an open licence to enable reproducibility and re-analysis. Negative impact / risks: (1) misuse to claim that LLM deliberations substitute for human deliberation, undermining democratic legitimacy; (2) over-reliance on these benchmarks for model selection without recognising that high deliberative-quality scores reflect surface text patterns, not normative virtues; (3) several topics include politically contested questions (constitutional reform, criminal justice, biobanking) and a naive reading of agent positions could be cited out of context to misrepresent model 'opinions'. Mitigations: explicit datasheet warnings, the requirement to cite the dataset's synthetic origin, and an authors' statement that this benchmark is not used to draw policy conclusions.
wasGeneratedBy: All records are synthetic and generated by the open-source deliberation_simulator framework (released alongside this submission, anonymised for double-blind review) using the OpenRouter API to access the listed LLMs. Per-run pipeline: (1) administer pre-deliberation DRI survey to each of N agents independently (N = group_size, typically 5); (2) run a free-flow group deliberation between agents over T turns (typically 10); (3) administer post-deliberation DRI survey; (4) compute group DRI score (Niemeyer et al. methodology); (5) optionally run AQuA discourse-quality assessment on the transcript via a separate LLM scorer. Survey items for the 12 topics are sourced from publicly documented citizen-assembly deliberations and stored in delib_sim/data/dri_surveys/surveys.xlsx in the framework repo. Sampling temperature = 0.0 in the main grid (varied 0.0/0.5/1.0 in the temp_study). Random seed = 42 for group assignment and persona shuffling. Time frame: November 2025 - March 2026. No human annotators were involved at any stage.

distribution.name: delibsim-bench-1.0.0-raw.tar.zst
distribution.description: Compressed archive of the full anonymised raw output tree. Decompress to obtain the original simulation_results/ folder layout: per-run config_used.yaml, deliberation_transcript_*_main.txt, deliberation_turn_log_*.json, dri_survey_prompts_pre/post_*.json, simulation_results_*.json, pilot_data_*.csv, dqi assessment JSONs, and per-batch study summary CSVs. Reasoning-trace transcripts (*_with_reasoning.txt) and DRI-distribution PNGs are excluded; all other files are included.
